body:
The specified BroadcastChannel behavior was [changed](https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/5305) to refrain from firing events on closed `BroadcastChannel`s.  Apparently this change was made because both Firefox and Chrome [seemed](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/5304#issuecomment-588238344) to behave this way.  [A](https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1622124) [few](https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1447586) [reports](https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1405911) indicate that the Firefox behavior was not actually deterministic, but Firefox has been [changed](https://hg.mozilla.org/mozilla-central/rev/b9badd1ee675) to align with the spec.

The [race with `close()` when posting from another thread](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/1371#issuecomment-223143001) and the deterministic behavior provided by a closed flag check at the receiver seem good reason for the BroadcastChannel spec change.  I expect the same reasoning would apply to MessagePort and consistency between BroadcastChannel and MessagePort [would be desirable](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/1371#issuecomment-224041642).

We could indeed add a step to the [message-port-post-message-steps](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/#message-port-post-message-steps), say a new Step 7.2, that could read`If finalTargetPort is not entangled, return.`, and I'm not sure if that is a good idea, for the following reason:

1. Calling `close` on the receiver could indeed set a local flag, and prevent further message events from being fired, however it would still not affect the other side. 
2. If you want `close` to have effect on both sides, you need to do a synchronous check on each send and each receive, which would somewhat change the semantics of the channel. 
3. I think the situation is different from broadcast channels, because their `closed` flag only affects the local channel, it doesn't affect other channels, or the abstract "broadcasting mechanism" operating globally. So moving the check to inside a task on the receiving event-loop, ensured this flag indeed is simply a piece of local state on a single event-loop, as opposed to something that would have to be checked synchronously potentially from other event-loops, and that was racy since it didn't allow for the flag changing while a message was in-flight. Fixing this in the spec was the reason for the change linked to. 
5. Since within the limits of the current semantics, calling `close` on a port cannot have an effect on the entangled port, it seems like a potentially confusing API, since it might give users the impression that calling it on the "receiving" end would actually prevent further messages from being sent by the entangled port. It would be clearer for code to simply ignore further messages if those are not expected.

Maybe it's still a good idea if this is what all the browsers are doing in practice. 

I think the way to potentially do it would be to spec an explicit flag, similar to `closed`, and have one for each port, making it clear that setting it to true only affect the local port(as opposed to the "entangled" concept, which without other convoluted changes would become racy under the expectation that calling `close` on one port would somehow affect that state across the channel). 

So I'd say the argument for doing this, if at all, shouldn't be consistency, since the situation is different. Thanks for checking out how that test holds-up in practice. Might be worth filing a few implementation bugs instead of adapting the spec to fit what is being done.

@gterzian whether we return early for sending or receiving doesn't matter from a theoretical perspective, right? There's nothing that exposes synchronously whether a port is entangled as far as I can tell.

> There's nothing that exposes synchronously whether a port is entangled as far as I can tell.

I think currently it's indeed not exposed, because there is no "entanglement" check at Step 7.x of message port post message steps.

Actually more broadly, it's not exposed as long as one "side" is always kept open by not having an explicit check of "entangledness" on both.  

So if we add such a check to both sides, then we would need to think really hard about what "disentangle"(step 2 of `close`) really means, or replace/enhance it with local flags on each end that would synchronously be affected by `close`(but not their remote counterparts). 

A longer explanation follows...

----

for example:

```js
// Message to the entangled, and already transferred, port. 
sendingPort.postMessage(...)

// "Dis-entangle" both ports
sendingPort.close()

// No-op, early return
sendingPort.postMessage(...)

// Make some assertions, using a previously setup second channel, 
// about whether the entangled port received the first message.
```

With the current spec, the first message will always still be received by the entangled port. Precisely because there is no check  for entangledness at step 7.x(inside the "receiver" task). 

The second message is not received, because of the early return at Step 6(and we can assume "dis-entangle" has immediate local effect on the sending side). 

So if we add a check for `targetPort` being entangled somewhere at Step 7.x, then the first message should also never be received(even though the task has already been queued, there should be an early return when the task is run preventing the event from firing). 

To re-iterate the potential bug described in this issue:

> The spec wording requires that messages posted **before close() is called on the receiving port** lead to events being fired even when that would happen after the close() call. This, however, is not necessarily what browsers do and is inconsistent with BroadcastChannel. 

So note this is from the perspective of calling `close` on the **receiver**. And yes we could indeed treat calling `close` on the receiver as immediately **locally** dis-entangling it, and add a check in Step 7.x to ensure no events are fired once `close` has been called, like:

```js
receiverPort.postMessage(...)

receiverPort.close()

// This is fine.
receiverPort.onmessage = assert_unreached().

// But what about the message sent earlier? Is that going to be received by the other side?
// Actually it would be interesting to see what implementations are currently doing.
```

So I think that's the big difference with `BroadcastChannel`, where "closing" is a purely local operation(actually we could compare "dis-entangled with immediate effect on both sides" to some hypothetical API on `BroadcastChannel` that would allow one channel to shut-down the broadcasting globally and synchronously). 

----

As a side note, we could precisely define "dis-entangle" to also include some sort of draining of the `port-message-queue` for both ports. And I think the only way to do that without races would be via synchronous IPC calls(in the cross-process case). I think for example FF went through great pains to remove sync IPC calls, and specifying something in a way that requires such operations might therefore not be a good idea. I personally like the current wording, which allows an implemention to be spec-compliant and yet fully non-blocking. 

A local "closed" flag on the receiver side might still be a good idea, if only because that seems to be what implementations are doing based on the research mentioned in this issue. Just to be clear I think it then should be a local flag, not something that ties into the "entangledness" of the channel as a whole.

It seems for `BroadcastChannel` you could also implement it as a local operation, but for efficiency you also want the messages to (eventually) stop.

When you send before you close I would expect it to still go out.

> When you send before you close I would expect it to still go out.

Then I think the way to do it is with a new `closed` flag that:

1. Would be set locally on a port when calling `close` on it(while still keeping the "dis-entangle" part as well)
2. would be checked in `postMessage` on "this port" as a new step 1, and result in an early return if true. 
3. Would be checked at step 7.1 of the message steps on `targetPort`, and would also result in an early return if true. 
4. Would not have any effect on the entangled port(but we'd keep the "dis-entangle" part as it is as an "it eventually happens" thing)
5. We might want to throw an "InvalidStateError" DOMException when the closed port is used with an `postMessage`. 

> for efficiency you also want the messages to (eventually) stop.

This would then be covered by the eventual "dis-entanglement" concept, where a call to `close` on either side would eventually dis-entangle the ports, and result in an early return at Step 6 of the message steps. 

----

The https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/#ports-and-garbage-collection could be supplemented to take such `closed` flag into account, since if the receiver has been closed then we don't care about references to it from tasks in it's message queue.

I would be in favor of a local "closed" flag that is checked on `this` at send and `finalTargetPort` at receive.

That would remove observability of the entangled check in `postMessage()`, which is problematic as a `close()` call on the receiving port may occur in another process/event-loop and there is no description to specify timing of a transfer in entangled state from one port to the other.

The same effect as a "closed" flag can be achieved by instead checking the existing [[Detached]] internal slot.  Checking the [[Detached]] slot would also provide what I assume is the intended behavior when `postMessage()` is called on a port for which "transfer steps" have already run but associated "transfer-receiving steps" for disentangle have not yet run.

AFAICS closing a `MessagePort` need only be a purely local operation, so I'm not seeing a big difference with `BroadcastChannel`.  The difference with `MessagePort` is that the "unclosed" port becomes useless.  Efficiencies regarding messages posted on the unclosed port are unobservable implementation details, and so the explicit disentangle on `close()` does not need to be specified.
@karlt @gterzian either of you interested in driving the change here? Probably the most effort here is writing web-platform-tests.

I would be interested. 

@karlt it's yours if you want it.  

To recap:

1. I think we agree on using "local" flags, one for each port. 
2. I agree it seems to make sense to re-use the `[[detached]]` slot as the "closed" flag, unless we feel it would be clearer to introduce a new and dedicated flag. 
3. I think we should keep the "entangled" wording next to it, to keep it consistent with the segment on GC and the definition of entanglement. When the dis-entanglement would exactly take effect would indeed not be directly noticeable by script.
4. We need to decide whether calling `postMessage` on a closed port throws an error, like it does for broadcast channel. I think it makes sense and obviously that's an API change(although it might not actually affect current WPT tests, since I don't think a lot of them would close a port and then use it to send messages after).

I would be very happy if you are able to sort this out, thank you @gterzian.

I can probably help with writing tests, if you like, but I can't promise exactly when I'd get to that given other distractions.

>     4. We need to decide whether calling `postMessage` on a closed port throws an error, like it does for broadcast channel.

There's support in https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/4265 for throwing an error, and doing so seems reasonable to me.

> I can probably help with writing tests, if you like, but I can't promise exactly when I'd get to that given other distractions.

Thanks, I will let you know if I need help. I'll try to keep the tests minimal if possible, since `close` should be a local only operation.

> The disentangling on close() can have some unfortunate interactions with postMessage() and "transfer-receiving steps".

Yes that's interesting.

 So because the entangled port is stored into the `remotePort` variable for the duration of the transfer, even if the ports are "dis-entangled" during the transfer due to a call to `close` on the one that isn't being transferred, they will be re-entangled as part of the transfer receive steps of the other. 

Actually I think this is a problem because `mc.port2` is still "entangled" until the transfer receive steps are run, when it will be dis-entangled when `shipped` is instead entangled with `ms.port1`. 

Actually maybe we should re-consider the use of `closed` flag, or that of checking the `[[Detached]]` slot, and instead define each port as having:

1. a `portMessageQueue` member, which is a reference to the queue of the local port. 
2. a `entangledPortMessageQueue`, which is a reference to the queue of the remote port. 

and where:

A. Transfer would take both refs out of the port, move it into the data holder. 
B. Receive would take them out of the data holder, move them into a new "transfer received" port. 
C. `close` would nullify both references, if they haven't been nullified already due to a transfer. 
D. `postMessage` would simply add a task directly to `entangledPortMessageQueue`, if not null. 
E. Whenever there are no reference left to a queue, or the only reference is via a `entangledPortMessageQueue` one, it can be GC'ed. Any port whose `portMessageQueue` is null, or if it is empty and there are no other references to it, can also be GC'ed.

That may be a solution.  I filed https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/5850 as it was feeling like this was getting beyond what was originally reported here.  That's at least another testcase to consider.
Good idea, I'll focus on the `closed` "flag"(or simply re-using the `detached` slot) first.
